authority: Cambridge Principal Examiner Reports for Teachers, 9618, June 2021 to November 2025, AS papers 11-13 and 21-23 only (60 report sections). Each entry is a confusion the reports state candidates made.
derivation_policy: Curated by hand from the located error statements and restated in our words. No examiner-report wording appears in learner-facing output.
how_to_use: Every entry earns one MISCON card on its objective. A MISCON card is a DISCRIMINATION: the error, the correct idea, and the test that tells them apart (the test field).

kinds.adjacent_concept: Two different concepts that sit near each other in the syllabus.
kinds.near_neighbour_term: Two terms that share most of their wording.
kinds.wrong_angle_same_concept: The right concept answered from the wrong angle, or a step of it done wrongly.

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of binary magnitudes and the difference between binary prefixes and decimal prefixes
entries.a: a kibibyte is 1000 bytes, or a tebibyte is 1024 gigabytes
entries.b: binary prefixes (kibi, mebi, gibi, tebi) step by 1024; decimal prefixes (kilo, mega, giga, tera) step by 1000
entries.test: Does the prefix contain "bi"? Then it is a power of 2 and each step is 1024 of the unit below it, named with the binary prefix.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /kibi|mebi|gibi|tebi|prefix/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of different number systems
entries.a: converting a denary number to plain 8-bit binary when BCD is asked for
entries.b: Binary Coded Decimal gives each denary digit its own 4-bit group
entries.test: Count the digits: a BCD answer has one 4-bit group per denary digit and no group above 1001.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /\bBCD\b|Binary Coded Decimal/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of different number systems
entries.a: reading a two’s complement value as if it were unsigned, or losing the minus sign
entries.b: in two’s complement the most significant bit carries a negative place value
entries.test: If the leftmost bit is 1, the value must come out negative; a positive answer means the MSB was read as positive.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /two.s complement|unsigned integer|minus sign/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of different number systems
entries.a: writing the denary values of hexadecimal digits side by side
entries.b: each hexadecimal digit is multiplied by its place value (16, 1) and the products added
entries.test: Hex 96 is 9 x 16 + 6 = 150, not "9" followed by "6"; an answer that just joins digits has skipped the place values.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /hexadecimal (place|digit)|appended/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of and be able to represent character data in its internal binary form, depending on the character set used
entries.a: extended ASCII holds 255 characters, or ASCII uses 7 bytes per character
entries.b: extended ASCII uses 8 bits per character, so 256 codes (0 to 255); ASCII uses 7 bits
entries.test: Number of codes = 2 to the power of the bits; the highest code is one less than the number of codes.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /ASCII/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of how data for a bitmapped image are encoded
entries.a: image resolution and colour depth used as if they were the same thing
entries.b: image resolution is the number of pixels (width x height); colour (bit) depth is the bits stored per pixel
entries.test: Which one changes if you add colours but keep the same pixels? That is colour depth.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /resolution|bit depth|colour depth/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of the effects of changing elements of a bitmap image on the image quality and file size
entries.a: changing the screen resolution changes the size of the image file
entries.b: the file stores the image resolution; the screen resolution is a property of the display
entries.test: Would the file change if the same file were opened on a different monitor? No, so screen resolution is not stored in it.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /screen resolution/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of how data for a vector graphic are encoded
entries.a: a drawing list is every shape that can be drawn
entries.b: a drawing list is the set of drawing objects that make up this particular image, each with its properties
entries.test: Could the list be used to redraw this image and only this image? Then it is the drawing list, not a library of shapes.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /drawing list|drawing object|library of shapes/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of how sound is represented and encoded
entries.a: sampling resolution confused with image resolution, or with sampling rate
entries.b: sampling rate is samples per second; sampling resolution is the bits stored per sample
entries.test: Rate is "how often", resolution is "how precisely": one is measured in hertz, the other in bits.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /sampl\w+ (rate|resolution)|image resolution/

entries.objective_text: Perform calculations to estimate the file size for a bitmap image
entries.a: leaving a file size in bits when the answer asks for bytes
entries.b: bits divide by 8 to give bytes before any prefix is applied
entries.test: Check the unit asked for; the colour depth is in bits, so a file size in bytes has a division by 8 in it.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /division by 8|bits to bytes|bits instead of bytes|8 bits/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of how a text file, bitmap image, vector graphic and sound file can be compressed
entries.a: describing run-length encoding of characters when the question is about an image, or the reverse
entries.b: RLE on a bitmap stores runs of same-coloured pixels; on text it stores runs of the same character
entries.test: Name what repeats in this file: pixels of one colour, or characters.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /pixels|characters|run-length|RLE/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of lossy and lossless compression and justify the use of a method in a given situation
entries.a: describing the effect of lossy compression when a method was asked for
entries.b: a method says what is removed (for example, detail the eye or ear is least sensitive to); an effect says what the result looks or sounds like
entries.test: Does the answer say what the compression does to the data? Then it is a method.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /lossy|lossless/

entries.objective_text: Explain the use of IP addresses in the transmission of data over the internet
entries.a: public and private IP addresses treated as the same kind of address
entries.b: a private IP address is used inside a local network and is not unique on the internet; a public IP address is unique on the internet
entries.test: Can a device on the other side of the world reach it directly? Then it is public.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /public|private IP/

entries.objective_text: Explain the use of IP addresses in the transmission of data over the internet
entries.a: IPv6 has six groups, or uses semicolons
entries.b: IPv6 is eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons; a double colon replaces runs of zero groups
entries.test: Count the groups and check the separator: eight, colons.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /IPv6|colon/

entries.objective_text: Describe the role and function of a router in a network
entries.a: data is sent in "packages"
entries.b: the unit of data on a network is a packet
entries.test: Use the technical term; "package" is not credited.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /package/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of the bus, star, mesh and hybrid topologies
entries.a: drawing a bus or mesh when a star is described, or mixing star and mesh
entries.b: a star connects every device to one central device; a mesh connects devices to several others
entries.test: Remove the central device: in a star every link fails, in a mesh the others still connect.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /star|mesh|bus topology/

entries.objective_text: Describe the hardware that is used to support a LAN
entries.a: a (wireless) network interface card gives the device its IP address
entries.b: a NIC or WNIC carries a unique MAC address; the IP address is assigned on the network
entries.test: Which address is fixed in the hardware? The MAC address.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /MAC address|WNIC|NIC/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of cloud computing
entries.a: a public cloud means anyone can see the data; a private cloud means only one person can
entries.b: public and private describe who the service is provided for and shared with, not who can read a user’s data
entries.test: Who owns and shares the infrastructure? That, not access to your files, is what public and private mean.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /public cloud|private cloud/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of the need for input, output, primary memory and secondary (including removable) storage
entries.a: memory and storage used interchangeably
entries.b: memory is primary (RAM, ROM) and directly accessed by the processor; storage is secondary and keeps data when power is off
entries.test: Does the processor read it directly while running? Memory. Does it keep files between sessions? Storage.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /memory|storage/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of the use of buffers
entries.a: the buffer sends the data
entries.b: a buffer is an area of memory that holds data temporarily; a processor moves data in and out of it
entries.test: A buffer cannot act. Name the component that does the sending.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /buffer/

entries.objective_text: Describe the principal operations of hardware devices
entries.a: describing lasers and pits for a magnetic hard disk
entries.b: a magnetic disk records data as magnetised regions read by a head; an optical disc uses a laser and pits
entries.test: Is the data magnetic or optical? The reading mechanism follows from that.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /optical|magnetic/

entries.objective_text: Show an understanding of monitoring and control systems
entries.a: the microprocessor and the actuator given each other’s role, or feedback read as user opinion
entries.b: the microprocessor decides; the actuator acts; feedback is the system’s output changing its next input
entries.test: Which part moves something physical? The actuator. Where does feedback come from? The system’s own output.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /actuator|feedback|microprocessor/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of embedded systems
entries.a: calling a device an embedded system on the grounds that it controls something
entries.b: an embedded system is a computer built into a larger device to do a dedicated task; control is something some embedded systems do
entries.test: Is the computer part of the device and dedicated to it? Then it is embedded, whether or not it controls anything.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /embedded/

entries.objective_text: Use the following logic gate symbols:
entries.a: drawing the NOR symbol for XOR, or the reverse
entries.b: XOR has a second curved line at the input side; NOR has a small circle at the output
entries.test: Look at the output: a circle means an inverted output (NAND, NOR).
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /XOR|NOR/

entries.objective_text: Construct a logic circuit
entries.a: replacing (NOT A) AND (NOT B) with one NAND gate
entries.b: (NOT A) AND (NOT B) is not NAND; build the circuit exactly as the expression is written
entries.test: Complete a truth table for both: they disagree when exactly one input is 1.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /NAND|NOT gates?/

entries.objective_text: Construct a truth table
entries.a: misreading where the brackets fall, or leaving out the final NOT
entries.b: work outwards from the innermost bracket, one column per sub-expression
entries.test: Add a column for each bracket before the output column; an output that is the exact opposite usually lost a NOT.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /bracket|final NOT|opposite/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of the purpose and role of registers, including the difference between general purpose and special purpose registers
entries.a: the program counter counts the instructions executed
entries.b: the program counter stores the memory address of the instruction that will be fetched next
entries.test: Is the value an address? It must be, because it is copied to the MAR in the fetch.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /Program Counter/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of the purpose and roles of the Arithmetic and Logic Unit (ALU), Control Unit (CU) and system clock, Immediate Access Store (IAS)
entries.a: describing the whole CPU when the control unit was asked for
entries.b: the control unit is one part of the CPU: it decodes instructions and sends control signals
entries.test: Remove the ALU and registers: what is left to do? That is the CU’s job.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /\bCU\b|control unit/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of how data are transferred between various components of the computer system using the address bus, data bus and control bus
entries.a: saying that data or instructions travel on the control bus
entries.b: the data bus carries data and instructions; the address bus carries addresses; the control bus carries control and timing signals
entries.test: Name what travels: an address, a value, or a signal such as read or write.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /bus/

entries.objective_text: Describe the stages of the Fetch-Execute (F-E) cycle
entries.a: copying the MAR’s own value into the MDR during the fetch
entries.b: the value stored at the memory address held in the MAR is what goes into the MDR ([MDR] ← [[MAR]])
entries.test: Square brackets mean "contents of"; two pairs mean "contents of the address held in".
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /MAR|MDR|register transfer|bracket/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of the purpose of interrupts
entries.a: one interrupt service routine handles every interrupt
entries.b: each cause of interrupt has its own service routine; the processor checks the interrupt’s priority before servicing it
entries.test: Would a printer out of paper and a keyboard press need the same code? No.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /ISR|Interrupt Service|priority/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of and be able to use different modes of addressing
entries.a: treating an immediate value as an address, or an address as a value
entries.b: #n is the number n itself (immediate); a bare address means the contents of that location (direct)
entries.test: Is there a # in front? Then use the number. No #? Look up the memory location.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /immediate|denary|contents of (the )?(memory|address)|#/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of and be able to use different modes of addressing
entries.a: in indexed addressing, adding IX to the value stored at the given address
entries.b: indexed addressing adds the index register to the address given, then uses the contents of that calculated address
entries.test: Add first, look up second.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /indexed/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of and perform binary shifts
entries.a: a cyclic shift given for a logical shift, or bits shifted the wrong way
entries.b: a logical shift discards the bits that fall off and fills with zeros; a cyclic shift moves them round to the other end
entries.test: Do any bits reappear at the other end? Only in a cyclic shift. Left multiplies, right divides.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /cyclic|logical shift|left|right/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of and perform binary shifts
entries.a: an arithmetic right shift that does not copy the sign bit
entries.b: an arithmetic shift keeps the sign bit and copies it into the vacated positions
entries.test: Shift a negative value: an arithmetic result must stay negative.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /sign bit|arithmetic/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of how bit manipulation can be used to monitor/control a device
entries.a: writing a mask of eight 1s as #1
entries.b: binary 1111 1111 is denary 255, so the immediate operand is #255 or B11111111
entries.test: Convert the mask before writing it with #.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /#1\b|#255|mask/

entries.objective_text: Explain the key management tasks carried out by the Operating System
entries.a: describing file management, or utilities such as defragmentation, when memory management was asked for
entries.b: memory management allocates and protects RAM for running processes; file management organises storage
entries.test: Is it about RAM while programs run, or files on a disk? The first is memory management.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /memory management|file management|defrag/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of the need for typical utility software provided with an Operating System
entries.a: defragmentation reduces the file size
entries.b: defragmentation moves the parts of each file together on the disk so they can be read faster; the file size is unchanged
entries.test: Does the amount of data change? No, only where it sits.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /defrag|disk formatter/

entries.objective_text: Explain why a computer system requires an Operating System (OS)
entries.a: the operating system’s security role described as what anti-virus software or a firewall does
entries.b: the operating system’s own security management covers user accounts, access rights and passwords
entries.test: Is it part of the operating system, or a separate program that runs on it?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /anti-virus|firewall|virus checker/

entries.objective_text: Describe features found in a typical Integrated Development Environment (IDE)
entries.a: context-sensitive prompts, dynamic syntax checking and auto-completion treated as one feature
entries.b: a context-sensitive prompt suggests what can come next; dynamic syntax checking flags errors as you type; auto-completion finishes a word
entries.test: Is it suggesting, checking, or finishing?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /context.sensitive|dynamic syntax|auto.complet/

entries.objective_text: Describe features found in a typical Integrated Development Environment (IDE)
entries.a: naming coding tools when debugging tools were asked for
entries.b: debugging tools include breakpoints, single stepping and variable watch windows; prompts and pretty printing help write code
entries.test: Does the feature help find a fault in running code? Then it is a debugging tool.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /debug|pretty print|breakpoint/

entries.objective_text: Explain the benefits and drawbacks of using either a compiler or interpreter and justify the use of each
entries.a: the interpreter fixes the errors
entries.b: an interpreter stops at an error so the programmer can fix it
entries.test: Software reports errors; people correct them.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /interpreter/

entries.objective_text: Explain the difference between the terms security, privacy and integrity of data
entries.a: security and integrity explained the wrong way round
entries.b: security protects data from loss or unauthorised access; integrity is data being accurate and consistent; privacy is who is allowed to see it
entries.test: Could the data be perfectly secure and still wrong? Yes, so they are different properties.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /integrity|security|privacy/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of the threats to computer and data security posed by networks and the internet
entries.a: phishing and pharming described as each other
entries.b: phishing uses a message to trick the user into visiting a fake site or giving details; pharming redirects the user to a fake site without their action
entries.test: Did the user click something in a message? Phishing. Were they redirected though they typed the right address? Pharming.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /phishing|pharming/

entries.objective_text: Describe security methods designed to protect the security of data
entries.a: encryption makes data unreadable, or verifies that data is authentic
entries.b: encryption makes intercepted data impossible to understand without the key; it does not stop interception or prove who sent it
entries.test: Can the data still be intercepted? Yes, so encryption protects meaning, not access.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /encrypt/

entries.objective_text: Describe how data validation and data verification help protect the integrity of data
entries.a: validation or verification makes sure data is correct
entries.b: validation checks data is reasonable and follows rules; verification checks it was copied accurately; neither proves it is true
entries.test: Could a wrong date of birth pass both? Yes, if it is a real date typed accurately.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /validation|verification|correct/

entries.objective_text: Describe how data validation and data verification help protect the integrity of data
entries.a: check digits and parity checks treated as the same check
entries.b: a check digit is calculated from the other digits of a code and validates entry; a parity bit checks transmitted bits
entries.test: Is the check on a typed code, or on bits sent over a link?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /check digit|parity/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of the different types of software licencing and justify the use of a licence for a given situation
entries.a: free software and freeware treated as the same thing
entries.b: free software (Free Software Foundation) gives the freedom to study, change and share the source; freeware is only free of charge
entries.test: Can you see and change the source code? Then it is free software, not just freeware.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /freeware|free software|shareware|open source/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of the need for copyright legislation
entries.a: describing plagiarism, or breaking copyright, as what copyright is
entries.b: copyright is the legal right of the creator to control copying and use of their work
entries.test: Is the answer about the right, or about breaking it?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /copyright|plagiarism/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of and use the terminology associated with a relational database model
entries.a: using "table" and "database" as if they meant the same thing, or calling a tuple a row of the database
entries.b: a database is made up of tables; a tuple is one row of one table; an entity is what a table stores data about
entries.test: Can a database contain several of it? Then it is a table.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /table|database|tuple|entity/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of and use the terminology associated with a relational database model
entries.a: giving primary keys when foreign keys were asked for
entries.b: a foreign key is an attribute in one table that is the primary key of another, and it links the two
entries.test: Does it point at another table? Foreign key.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /foreign key|primary key/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of the limitations of using a file- based approach for the storage and retrieval of data
entries.a: data dependency given where program-data dependency was meant
entries.b: program-data dependency means a change to the file structure forces changes to every program that uses it
entries.test: Name what depends on what: the programs depend on the structure of the data.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /dependenc/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of the features provided by a Database Management System (DBMS) that address the issues of a file based approach
entries.a: access rights and views treated as the same feature
entries.b: access rights control which operations a user may perform; a view controls which data a user is shown
entries.test: Is it about what the user can do, or what the user can see?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /access rights|views/

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of how software tools found within a DBMS are used in practice
entries.a: describing an IDE when the DBMS developer interface was asked for
entries.b: the developer interface lets a developer create and manipulate the database structure and build forms, queries and reports
entries.test: Is it part of the DBMS, working on the database? Then it is the developer interface.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /IDE|developer interface/

entries.objective_text: Write an SQL script to query or modify data (DML) which are stored in (at most two) database tables
entries.a: SUM used where COUNT is needed, or the reverse
entries.b: COUNT gives how many rows meet the condition; SUM adds up the values in a field
entries.test: Is the answer a number of records, or a total of amounts?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /\bSUM\b|\bCOUNT\b/

entries.objective_text: Understand given SQL (DDL) statements and be able to write simple SQL (DDL) statements using a sub-set of statements
entries.a: UPDATE TABLE for a change of structure, or CREATE TABLE for a new database
entries.b: ALTER TABLE changes a table’s structure; UPDATE changes data; CREATE DATABASE creates the database
entries.test: Structure or data? DDL changes structure, DML changes data.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /ALTER|UPDATE|CREATE (TABLE|DATABASE)/

entries.objective_text: Write an SQL script to query or modify data (DML) which are stored in (at most two) database tables
entries.a: quotation marks round a Boolean value, or none round a string
entries.b: string literals take quotation marks; Boolean and numeric values do not
entries.test: Check the field’s data type in the table definition first.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /quotation marks|Boolean|string comparison/

entries.objective_text: Show an understanding of abstraction
entries.a: abstraction and decomposition treated as the same process
entries.b: abstraction removes unnecessary detail; decomposition breaks a problem into sub-problems
entries.test: Is detail being left out, or is the problem being divided?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /abstraction|decomposition/

entries.objective_text: Describe and use decomposition
entries.a: decomposition breaks down an existing program
entries.b: decomposition breaks down a problem, leading to modules
entries.test: What is being broken down: the problem.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /decomposition|program/

entries.objective_text: Draw a flowchart from: • a structured English description • pseudocode
entries.a: a decision in a flowchart drawn without a diamond or without Yes/No labels
entries.b: every decision is a diamond with two labelled exits
entries.test: Count the exits and read their labels.
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /diamond|decision|flow ?lines?|shape/

entries.objective_text: Select and use appropriate data types for a problem solution
entries.a: a date stored as STRING, or a value in quotation marks given a numeric type
entries.b: DATE is a pseudocode data type; a value in quotation marks is a string or character
entries.test: Look for the quotation marks, then ask whether a date type exists: it does.

entries.objective_text: Show understanding of the purpose of a record structure to hold a set of data of different data types under one identifier

entries.objective_text: Write pseudocode to process array data
entries.a: comparing the index when the element was meant, or the reverse
entries.b: the index is the position; the element is the value stored at that position
entries.test: Write Data[i]: i is the index, Data[i] is the element.
